title: Can Solar Panels Be Recycled? The Complete 2026 Guide
excerpt: Yes, solar panels can be recycled — but the process is more complex than most homeowners realize. Here's what happens at end-of-life and what it means for your ROI.
content:
Can Solar Panels Be Recycled?

Yes — solar panels can be recycled, but the infrastructure to do so at scale is still developing in the United States. Approximately 90–95% of the materials in a standard silicon solar panel are recoverable: the aluminum frame, glass, copper wiring, and silver contacts are all recyclable. The challenge is the encapsulant — a plastic layer that bonds the silicon cells to the glass — which makes separation energy-intensive.

What Solar Panels Are Made Of

A standard crystalline silicon panel contains: tempered glass (about 75% of weight), aluminum frame (10%), silicon solar cells (3%), polymer encapsulant (10%), and copper, silver, and other metals (2%). Of these, glass and aluminum are easy to recycle through conventional streams. Silicon and the precious metals require specialized processing to recover economically.

How Solar Panel Recycling Works

The current primary method is mechanical recycling: panels are shredded, and materials are separated by density and chemistry. A more advanced thermal process heats panels to burn off the encapsulant, allowing clean recovery of glass and cells. The thermal method recovers more value but uses more energy. A handful of US companies — including We Recycle Solar and SOLV Energy — offer panel take-back programs for residential customers.

Does This Affect Your Solar ROI?

For most homeowners, the short answer is no — not meaningfully. Solar panels last 25–30 years, and recycling costs at end-of-life are typically $15–45 per panel. A 6kW home system has roughly 15–18 panels, so worst-case end-of-life recycling costs around $500–800. Against 25 years of electricity savings averaging $15,000–30,000 depending on your city, this is less than 3% of lifetime value.

State Recycling Programs

Washington state was the first US state to pass extended producer responsibility legislation for solar panels (2017). California has landfill restrictions on solar panels, classifying them as universal waste. Most other states currently have no specific solar recycling mandates, meaning panels often end up in general landfills — something the industry is working to change.

What You Should Do

When buying solar, ask your installer about their end-of-life panel disposal policy. Reputable installers partner with recyclers and will handle removal and disposal when you eventually replace your system. The bigger priority right now is choosing the right system for your city — recycling logistics 25 years from now matter far less than whether solar makes financial sense for you today.
